items.stem: A medical student is alone with a patient who says: 'I feel so much better — can you put in a good word with the team about going home today?' The student has not been briefed on this patient's risk. Which response is most appropriate?

options.t: Affirm to the patient that she appears improved and will relay this to the team, then complete a brief suicide screen to provide the team with an update.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Affirming improvement to the patient and conducting an independent assessment crosses the student role boundary — the student cannot produce or communicate a dispositive safety determination.

options.t: Explain that discharge is the team's decision, then conduct a full structured suicide risk assessment using a standardized instrument and document findings independently.

trap.name: Student clears patient
trap.note: Conducting and independently documenting a solo risk assessment is well outside the student role — students report to the team, they do not clear patients.

options.t: Reassure the patient that the team is working toward discharge and provide the hospital's crisis line number.

trap.name: Reassure and defer
trap.note: Providing a crisis line to an admitted patient implies discharge is coming; the student is implying endorsement of a decision the team hasn't made, without any supervisory loop.

options.t: Tell the patient that discharge is the team's decision and that you will let the attending know she wants to discuss it — then inform the team promptly.

items.why: Student clears patient in two forms — direct affirmation and independent documentation — both cross the role boundary. The student's role is to ask, observe, and report to the team — not to clear a patient for discharge or to produce an independent safety assessment. Reassure and defer leaves the student in a limbo of implied endorsement without any supervisory loop.
items.pearl: Students can ask, observe, and report to the team — they cannot independently clear a patient for discharge or conduct a solo risk assessment.
items.evidence: pg_suicide.md 'Student Role' — You cannot: Clear a patient for discharge independently.

items.stem: A patient placed in physical restraints 4 hours ago following an agitation episode is now calm, cooperative, and asking to be released. His nurse pages the on-call student. Which of the following best reflects the correct management principle?

options.t: Continue the restraints through the end of the shift to ensure safety is maintained across the nursing team handoff.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Restraints are not a shift-duration safety measure — they must be discontinued the moment the patient is safe, regardless of shift timing.

options.t: Notify the attending immediately — the patient's calm state and request to be released require prompt reassessment; restraints must be discontinued as soon as the patient is safe, not held to shift end.
Ask the patient to demonstrate he can remain calm for 30 minutes, then release him and document the trial.

trap.name: Restraint as stability
trap.note: Imposing a time-contingent test before release inverts the standard — the principle is discontinue as soon as safe, not apply additional criteria.

options.t: Since the original physician order is still active, no action is needed until the order expires.

trap.name: Order = permission to continue
trap.note: A restraint order requires continuous time-limited review — a patient who is calm and requesting release must be reassessed immediately, not held to order expiration.

items.why: Restraint as stability in two forms and Order = permission both treat the order as a static permission. Restraint is a time-limited safety measure requiring a physician order, continuous monitoring, and discontinuation the moment the patient is safe — the page explicitly states 'not the end of a shift.' The student's correct action is immediate attending notification so the reassessment can happen.
items.pearl: Restraints require time-limited orders, continuous monitoring, and discontinuation as soon as the patient is safe — not the end of a shift.
items.evidence: agitation.md 'Restraint and seclusion' — They require a time-limited physician order, close and continuous monitoring, and discontinuation the moment the patient is safe — not the end of a shift.

items.stem: A team is debriefing after a physical restraint episode involving a Black patient on the inpatient unit. A student asks what the published evidence shows about racial disparities in restraint use in inpatient psychiatry. Which statement correctly reflects the data?

options.t: Black patients are restrained at similar rates to White patients after adjusting for clinical acuity — the apparent disparity is explained by severity of presentation.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The adjusted disparity persists after controlling for clinical factors — it is a quality-of-care issue, not an acuity artifact.

options.t: Black patients are more likely to receive verbal de-escalation before physical restraint — the data show greater resource deployment, not disparity.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The evidence shows the opposite — Black patients face higher adjusted odds of physical restraint, not more de-escalation.

options.t: Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of physical restraint on inpatient units — this disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not an acuity artifact.
Joint Commission non-discrimination standards adopted in 2015 have eliminated racial disparities in restraint use.

trap.name: No disparity exists
trap.note: The disparity is ongoing and documented — regulatory standards have not eliminated it.

items.why: No disparity exists in three forms. The page explicitly states: 'Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of physical restraint on inpatient units (and ~2.84× in the ED awaiting admission) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.' This is the only data point cited on the page for this topic and is explicitly framed as belonging in a post-restraint debrief.
items.pearl: Black patients face ~1.85× the adjusted odds of physical restraint on inpatient units — a quality-of-care disparity that belongs in every post-restraint debrief.
items.evidence: agitation.md 'Restraint and seclusion' — Black patients face roughly 1.85× the adjusted odds of physical restraint on inpatient units (and ~2.84× in the ED awaiting admission) — that disparity is a quality-of-care issue, not a footnote.

items.stem: A patient with mania is pacing loudly in the hallway, slamming cabinet doors, and making hostile comments toward staff. He has not made a direct threat or moved toward anyone. You are the student and the first person to encounter him. Which response is best?

options.t: Step calmly into the hallway — not blocking his exit — introduce yourself, acknowledge his frustration: 'I can see you're really upset right now. What's going on?' Then offer a choice of where to speak.
Return to the nursing station and request an involuntary IM medication order before approaching, so the team is ready to intervene.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Medication is not the default first step when verbal de-escalation has not been attempted and no imminent threat exists — the framework starts with presence and listening.

options.t: Stand in the doorway and firmly instruct him to return to his room or further action will be taken.

trap.name: Commands over choices
trap.note: Issuing a command removes the patient's sense of control — the de-escalation framework centers offering choices, not issuing directives.

options.t: Alert the restraint team and position staff at the hallway exits in case the patient escalates.

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Preemptively positioning the restraint team before de-escalation has been attempted violates least-restrictive principle when no imminent threat has occurred.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Commands over choices, and Restraint first are three forms of reaching for escalation before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework starts with calm presence, acknowledgment, genuine choices, and listening. The student also needs to stay near the exit and never block the patient's — personal safety and de-escalation are not competing goals.
items.pearl: Calm presence + acknowledging distress + offering choices = the first move in de-escalation; stay near your exit and never block the patient's.
items.evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with no psychiatric history, admitted for pneumonia, begins shouting at night and pulling at his oxygen tubing. He is combative with staff. The on-call resident asks the student how to approach this. What is the most appropriate first frame?

options.t: Start an antipsychotic immediately and then search for the cause — treating the agitation reduces the risk of self-harm while the workup proceeds.

trap.name: Agitation = antipsychotic
trap.note: Reaching for the antipsychotic before identifying the driver is the error — non-pharmacologic and cause-directed management comes first even in hyperactive presentations.

options.t: Initiate a CIWA-Ar protocol — nighttime agitation in an older admitted patient is most likely alcohol withdrawal.

trap.name: It's just withdrawal
trap.note: Alcohol withdrawal is on the differential but imposing a specific protocol before the actual driver is identified may apply the wrong treatment to the wrong cause.

options.t: Apply soft restraints and then assess — the agitation puts both the patient and staff at immediate risk.

trap.name: Restraint first
trap.note: Restraints are the last resort after lesser measures have failed or are clearly inadequate — applying them before cause-finding and de-escalation bypasses the entire ladder.

options.t: Name the question: 'What is driving this agitation?' — systematic evaluation for delirium, substance withdrawal, medication effects (akathisia, steroids), pain, hypoxia, urinary retention, and fear must precede any pharmacologic decision.

items.why: Agitation = antipsychotic, It's just withdrawal, and Restraint first all skip cause-finding. Agitation is a symptom. The standard is to name the driver — delirium, withdrawal, akathisia, pain, hypoxia, retention, fear — before selecting an intervention. Pharmacotherapy, if needed, then matches the cause.
items.pearl: Agitation is always a symptom — name the driver before selecting the intervention; the treatment should match the cause.
items.evidence: agitation.md 'Find the driver' — Before you decide what to do, ask what is producing this. The usual drivers are delirium, intoxication or withdrawal, an acute psychotic or manic process, akathisia, unrelieved pain, and a fear or trauma response. 'High-yield pearls' — Agitation is a symptom — always ask 'what is driving this?' before 'what do we give?'

tier2.q: Why does matching the treatment to the agitation driver matter so much in an older medical patient?

options.t: Older patients cannot metabolize antipsychotics — any dose will cause over-sedation regardless of indication.
Agitation in older patients is always fear-related — benzodiazepines are therefore the universal treatment.

The wrong treatment can worsen the driver: benzodiazepines deepen most delirium; antipsychotics can precipitate NMS in unexcluded catatonia; treating withdrawal incorrectly can cause seizures — mismatching agent to cause produces iatrogenic harm.
Pharmacotherapy is inappropriate in all older patients — verbal de-escalation is the only evidence-based approach regardless of driver.

tier2.why: It is a drug–driver matching principle. Benzodiazepines are correct for alcohol/sedative withdrawal and dangerous in most other delirium. Antipsychotics are appropriate for dangerous agitation in non-catatonic, non-LBD states and dangerous if catatonia or LBD is present. Analgesics resolve pain-driven agitation that no psychotropic would touch. The wrong drug in the wrong patient makes the agitation worse — the paradigm case being benzodiazepines deepening delirium in a delirious elder.
